title: Türkiye’s Geographical Indication Foods: How to Check Each Province’s Registered Specialities Before You Eat
excerpt: How to use Türkiye’s official geographical indication register to find the registered foods of each province on your route, read what the entries mean, and turn them into a realistic eating plan.

body.text: In early November 2026 local press in Hatay reported that Antakya coffee (Antakya kahvesi) had been registered as a geographical indication, describing it as the province’s 79th registered product. On 11 November Anadolu Ajansı reported that TÜRKPATENT, Türkiye’s patent and trademark office, had granted geographical indications to 102 products in the first ten months of 2026, bringing the national total to 1,912. For travellers this is more than trade news: the same public register that records these names is a free, official map of what each province considers its own. This guide explains what the labels mean, how to look a province up, and how to use the results to plan meals without turning your trip into a checklist.
What a geographical indication is, in plain terms

TÜRKPATENT’s [geographical indications portal](https://ci.turkpatent.gov.tr/sayfa/co%C4%9Frafi-i%C5%9Faret-nedir) defines a geographical indication (coğrafi işaret) as a sign that links a product to the place it comes from because of its distinctive qualities, reputation or other characteristics. It covers food and farm products but also mining products, handicrafts and industrial goods, so not every entry you find will be edible. There are two kinds of geographical indication, and a third, related label:

items: Designation of origin (menşe adı): the product’s qualities come essentially or entirely from the natural and human factors of one area, and production, processing and all other stages take place inside that area.

Geographical indication of source (mahreç işareti): the product is tied to an area by its reputation or other characteristics, and at least one stage of production or processing must happen there; other stages can take place elsewhere.

Traditional product name (geleneksel ürün adı): not an origin label at all, but a name that has been used in the market for at least 30 years for a product made in a traditional way. Anadolu Ajansı reports that Turkish coffee (Türk kahvesi) was registered in this category in 2026.

body.text: The portal’s [page for consumers](https://ci.turkpatent.gov.tr/sayfa/t%C3%BCketiciler-i%C3%A7in) adds one useful detail for shoppers: since January 2018, registered products are required to carry the matching emblem, so on packaged goods you may see a small designation-of-origin or geographical-indication logo next to the name.
How to look up a province in the official register

The register lives on TÜRKPATENT’s Coğrafi İşaretler Portalı (ci.turkpatent.gov.tr), which is in Turkish. When we checked it in November 2026, the portal’s province listing invited visitors to search geographical indications by province (“İl bazında coğrafi işaret arayabilirsiniz”), and the menu separates Coğrafi İşaretler (geographical indications) from Geleneksel Ürün Adları (traditional product names). The [database page](https://ci.turkpatent.gov.tr/veri-tabani) lists entries with the name, file number, application date, registration number, registration date, type (Türü), product group (Ürün grubu), province (İl) and status (Durumu).

Opening a single entry shows the same fields plus who registered it and a link to the registration certificate as a PDF. The registrant is often a local chamber of commerce or a municipality: Afyon kaymağı, for example, was registered by the Afyon Chamber of Commerce, and Afyon lokumu by Afyonkarahisar Municipality. Two practical tips: filter by province first and then scan the product group column to skip handicrafts and raw crops if you only care about dishes; and check the status column, which shows where each entry stands. Anadolu Ajansı reported that 805 applications were still being processed at the time of the 102 announcement. A brand-new registration such as Antakya coffee may be reported in the news before you can find it easily in the database, so search by name and treat the press report as your reference until the entry appears.
A four-step method for planning what to eat

items: List the provinces on your route, not just the cities. A province entry often covers district products, so a stop in Trabzon city can also mean products named after Akçaabat or Hamsiköy.

Pull the registered food entries for each province and sort them into three rough groups: dishes you sit down for (soups, mantı, kebabs), things you meet in the morning (breads, simit, kaymak, cheeses, sucuk) and things you buy by weight (honey, dried fruit, sweets).

Match each group to a moment of your day. Breakfast tables, bakeries and pastry shops, and market streets are where most visitors naturally meet the second and third groups; the first group needs a proper meal slot, so book it into the day you have most time in that city.
Pick two or three per stop and leave the rest. A long list is a temptation to rush; a short one lets you ask for a dish by its full name and notice how it differs from the version you know.

body.text: This is general guidance, not a timetable: what is served at breakfast, which bakery opens early and which dishes are seasonal vary by town, so ask your host or check locally on the day.
The entries below come from the register and from GoTürkiye, the official tourism portal. They are examples to show how the method works, not a complete list or a ranking.

items: Afyonkarahisar: Afyon kaymağı is registered as a designation of origin (2009), Afyon sucuğu as a geographical indication of source (2005) and Afyon lokumu as a geographical indication of source (2021). GoTürkiye’s [two-day Afyon gastronomy route](https://goturkiye.com/routes/2-day-gastronomy-route-in-afyonkarahisar) puts sucuk and kaymak on the breakfast table with village bread and notes that the city joined the UNESCO Creative Cities Network for gastronomy in 2019. See our [Afyon destination page](/destinations/afyon).

Kayseri: Kayseri mantısı is registered as a geographical indication of source in the dishes and soups group (2009). The 2026 batch reported by Anadolu Ajansı adds Kayseri purov mantısı and pöç kebabı. If your trip runs through Kayseri on the way to Cappadocia, a mantı lunch is an easy fit; our [private Cappadocia itinerary guide](/blog/private-turkiye-itinerary-cappadocia-guide) helps with the rest of the route.
Trabzon: Akçaabat köftesi (2010) and Hamsiköy sütlacı (2017) are both geographical indications of source, and the 2026 batch adds Trabzon dondurması. See the [Trabzon page](/destinations/trabzon).

Hatay: Antakya künefesi has been a registered geographical indication of source since 2008. The 2026 batch includes Hatay abugannuş, Hatay Arap kebabı, Hatay haytalı and Hatay müşebbek tatlısı, among 15 Hatay registrations this year.

Across the Aegean and Anatolia: GoTürkiye’s [list of GI-certified products](https://goturkiye.com/blog/7-gi-certified-turkish-products) includes Aydın figs, Malatya apricots, Taşköprü garlic from Kastamonu, Milas olive oil from Muğla and Bayramiç beyazı, a white nectarine from Çanakkale that it presents as a summer fruit.

body.text: Gaziantep has its own long list of registered foods, including several new 2026 entries; for how to pace a visit there, use our [Gaziantep food weekend guide](/blog/gaziantep-food-weekend-planning).
A practical note on Antakya coffee

According to Söz Gazetesi’s report of 9 November 2026, Antakya coffee is dark and double-roasted, known for its intense aroma, served in slim tea glasses rather than small coffee cups, and also called “süvari” locally. The practical point for a visitor is simply that it is not the same order as Turkish coffee: if you are in Antakya and want the local style, ask for it by name. Our [Hatay page](/destinations/hatay) covers the province more broadly.
What a geographical indication does not tell you

items: It is not a rating of a restaurant, café or shop. The register records a product name, its type and who registered it; it says nothing about which kitchen makes it well today.

TÜRKPATENT describes the system as a quality sign tied to origin and characteristics, but an entry does not tell you whether a particular plate or jar in front of you meets that description. Look for the emblem on packaged goods and use your own judgement in restaurants.

Registration in Türkiye is a national record. Registration in the European Union is a separate process; GoTürkiye notes, for example, that Milas olive oil was the first Turkish olive oil to receive an EU geographical indication mark, but you should not assume any other product has one.
It does not give seasons, opening hours or prices. A registered summer fruit will not be on the stall in January, and some dishes are only made in particular homes or months.
A missing entry does not mean a town has nothing special. Many local dishes are not registered, and hundreds of applications were still being processed in late 2026.
Write down every province (il) your route passes through, including overnight stops.
Search each one on the TÜRKPATENT portal and note the food entries, their type and status.
Keep the Turkish names exactly as registered; they are what you will say when ordering.
Sort the list into breakfast and bakery items, sit-down dishes, and things sold by weight.
Choose two or three per stop and assign them to a meal you actually have time for.
For packaged products, look for the designation-of-origin or geographical-indication emblem.
Treat brand-new registrations from the news as provisional until you can see the entry.

body.text: Used this way, the register is less a list of trophies and more a conversation starter: it tells you which names a province has chosen to protect, and that is often the quickest way into its kitchen. If you want ideas for quieter stops where these products are part of everyday life, our [hidden gems guide](/blog/hidden-gems-turkiye-most-tourists-never-find) is a good next read.

seo.intent: Find and verify the registered geographical indication foods of each province on a Türkiye route and use them to plan meals.
seo.uniqueValue: A traveller’s method for reading TÜRKPATENT’s official register by province, with sourced example entries and a clear account of what a geographical indication does and does not tell you.
